belt: Hi — I'm ready to start Define on our project.

reply.answer:
Welcome — I'm here to coach you and your team through your improvement project step by step, so you don't need to be an expert. We'll work through five phases together:
• Define — pin down the problem and who's solving it
• Measure — get the real numbers
• Analyse — find the true root cause
• Improve — test and apply the fix
• Control — make the gains stick
Right now we're in Define — the most important phase, because a clear problem is half the solution. For each of the thirteen parts I'll explain what it is and why it matters, show you a finished example, then ask for yours. When all thirteen are agreed, you and your team review the Define report and approve it.

Let's start with the first step: the business case. The business case says why this project deserves time and people: what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and what it costs. It is what earns the project its support. People outside the team only back what they can understand and size — and it is the first thing the Define report shows.
reply.explanation: The business case explains why the project matters and earns its support.
reply.example:
Sample only — to show the form of a good answer. Do not copy it; answer for your own process.
"During January to June 2026, 12% of invoices produced by UK billing were returned for correction, against 3% for the rest of the group. The rework and delayed payments cost about €35k a month."
reply.prompt: Why is your project worth doing? Tell me what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and roughly what it costs.

Now let's move to the next step: defining the project team. 

The project team identifies who leads, who sponsors, who owns the process, and who does the work — each with a name, a role, and what they will do. This matters because improvement projects need people before they need work. The champion clears obstacles, and the process owner keeps the result after the project ends; without them, a good fix fades.

Illustration (not your data): "Leader: Anna (Green Belt, runs the project). Champion: Mark, Finance Director (approves, removes blockers). Process owner: Jo, Billing Manager (owns the process). Now let’s move to the Voice of the Customer (VOC) and Critical-to-Quality requirements (CTQs). These define who receives what your process produces, what they need, and how you measure meeting those needs. 

What it is: The Voice of the Customer asks who receives the output from your process — inside the company, outside, or both — and what they need or complain about most. CTQs turn those needs into measurable requirements. For example, if customers say they want invoices accurate and on time, CTQs could be “invoice amount matches the agreed price on 100% of lines” and “invoice sent within 2 working days of the order.”

Why it matters: It keeps the project honest. We improve what matters to the people receiving the output, and a CTQ is how "they want it accurate" becomes a requirement you can check.

Illustration (not your data): "Customers: client finance teams (external) and our credit control (internal). They need invoices that are correct and on time; the top complaint is wrong amounts. CTQs: invoice amount matches the agreed price on 100% of lines; invoice sent within 2 working days of the order."

Prompt: Who are the customers of your process, and what do they need or complain about most? For each need, how would you measure that it is met?
reply.explanation: The Voice of the Customer identifies who receives the process output and what they need; CTQs turn those needs into measurable requirements.

Now that the VOC summary is confirmed, let's move to the next step: the problem statement. This is the heart of the Define phase. It captures what is going wrong, where it happens, since when, who is affected, why it matters to them, how the problem shows up, and how big it is. Together, these are called the 5W2H: What, Where, When, Who, Why, How, and How much.

Why it matters: A clear problem statement keeps everyone focused on solving the same issue. It describes the problem only — never its cause or its fix. This precision is essential for the team to move forward with confidence.

Illustration (not your data):
| Question | How it is formulated | Example |
|---|---|---|
| What | the defect, in one noun phrase | invoices returned for correction |
| Where | the process, the step(s) where it shows, and the place | UK billing, order to invoice — at "Generate invoice" |
| When | the period, or since when | January to June 2026 |
| Who | who is affected | client finance teams, credit control |
| Why | why it matters to them | wrong amounts delay payment and trust |
| How | how the defect shows up | clients return the invoice or dispute it |
| How much | the size, against a requirement | 12% of invoices, against 3% elsewhere |

Now we’re moving to the next step: the baseline estimate. This is where we define the project’s primary metric — the measure of the defect that says whether the project succeeded — and where it stands today.

**What it is:** A metric is something you can count the same way twice. For example, 'invoice quality' isn’t one — two people would score it differently. 'The share of invoices returned by collections for correction' is: you can point at any invoice and say yes or no.

**Why it matters:** This is the number your whole project is judged on. Define sets it, Measure proves it, Control compares against it. If the definition shifts between phases, nothing downstream compares.

**How to read it:** A usable Define baseline has three parts: a number, the period it covers, and where it came from. 'About 12%' is a start; '12% of invoices returned, January to June, from the collections log' is something we can go and check.

**Illustration (not your data):** Primary metric: invoice error rate — %, the share of invoices returned by clients for correction. Baseline: 12%, January to June 2026, from the collections log. It feeds the finance KPI days-sales-outstanding.

**Prompt:** What is the one measure of the defect that will say whether the project succeeded? What unit is it in, what exactly does it count, and which business KPI does it feed? Where does it stand today — and which data is that number from?
reply.explanation: The baseline estimate defines the primary metric to measure the project's success.

define_structured.business_case: Across our three hospital sites, 23% of supplier invoices were paid after their 30-day terms from January to June 2026. Late payments to our suppliers are costing us: we paid about £62,000 in late-payment interest and lost early-payment discounts last year, and three key medical suppliers put us on stop twice this year, which held up ward stock. To add detail: this is based on the AP ledger for January to June 2026, across all three hospital sites, and the finance director has agreed it.

define_structured.voc_summary: Our customers are the suppliers, who need paying on the agreed 30-day terms, and our own ward managers, who need stock to keep arriving. Suppliers complain most about payments arriving late and not knowing when they will be paid; ward managers about deliveries being held. One more thing: suppliers also told us they cannot see the status of an invoice once it is submitted.

critical_to_quality.need: paid within 30 days of the invoice date
critical_to_quality.requirement: paid within 30 days of the invoice date on every invoice
no supplier puts us on stop in a quarter

define_structured.problem_statement: Since January 2026, 23% of supplier invoices processed by the accounts payable team across our three hospital sites have been paid late — measured January to June 2026. This issue delays stock for ward managers, incurs interest and lost discounts, and has led to supplier stops, with late invoices waiting at 'resolve mismatches' and 'approve.' Suppliers chase payment by phone and email, and some put us on stop.

baseline_estimate.raw: One metric: late payment rate, in %, meaning the share of supplier invoices paid more than 30 days after the invoice date. It is about 23% today, from the AP ledger for January to June 2026. It feeds our finance KPI, creditor days.

metric_definitions.name: late_payment_rate
metric_definitions.meaning: The share of supplier invoices paid more than 30 days after the invoice date.

project_scope.in_scope: Invoice receipt to payment release for purchase-order invoices at our three hospital sites.
project_scope.out_scope: Non-PO invoices, payroll, procurement tendering, and the ERP system itself.

define_structured.goal_statement: Reduce the late payment rate from 23% to under 5% by 31 March 2027, and keep it under 5% for three months after that.

target_value.raw: Late payment rate: under 5% of supplier invoices.

define_structured.target_date: We plan to finish the project by 31 March 2027 (2027-03-31).

result.calculation_note: (23% baseline − 5% target) × 42000 units/year × 9 per unit = 68040 a year. Check the units agree: the rates are shares of the yearly volume, and the unit cost is the cost of one defect.

benefits_analysis.cost_of_gap: About £68,000 a year in interest and lost discounts, from the savings calculation.
benefits_analysis.realisation_schedule: It would start in Q2 2027 at about £17,000 a quarter.
benefits_analysis.finance_contact: Sam Reid, management accountant, who will validate it.

define_structured.secondary_metrics: Two things must not get worse: the number of supplier payment queries the AP team handles each month, and AP staff overtime hours. Both should stay at or below today's levels.
